notes: Ruling slot 23 = Barakzai (Musahiban) dynasty of Zahir Shah. PDPA split: Parcham (Moscow-favoured, national-democratic front) in 4, Khalq (radical class-struggle wing) in 5. Daoud's circle in 7 (Soviet-leaning authoritarian modernizer), Etemadi cabinet in 13. Afghan Mellat kept in 3 per MD (ASDP). Pashtunistan irredentists in 6 because Moscow backs the claim against US-allied Pakistan. Shola-e Javid (Maoist) in 19; Setam-e Melli in 18.

0.name: Halqa-ye Sardār Wali
0.text:
The court's hard-line royalists gather around General Abdul Wali, the king's cousin and son-in-law, who commands the Central Forces garrisoning Kabul. On 1 January 1970 he is widely seen as the strongman behind the throne, the guardian of the dynasty's grip on the capital and the main rival of the sidelined Sardar Daoud.

The circle wants the New Democracy kept on a short leash: parliament may talk, but the palace and the army decide. It distrusts the dependence on Moscow created by Soviet arms and aid, and looks to Washington, Bonn and Tehran for money and equipment. Its leverage is the Kabul garrison, the royal family and the king's ear.

1.name: Dimokrāsi-ye Naw
1.text:
The reformers who drafted the 1964 constitution, which barred the royal family from ministerial office and created an elected parliament, call their project New Democracy. Former ministers, judges and Western-educated professors, they hold posts in the ministries, the courts and Kabul University, but they have no party of their own, since the king has never signed the law permitting parties.

They want parties legalised, provincial councils elected and the rule of law entrenched, while keeping the monarchy and Islam as anchors of stability. They favour American, West German and World Bank aid as a counterweight to Moscow. Their leverage is expertise and royal patronage; their weakness is the absence of any mass following.

2.name: Hezb-e Demokrāt-e Motaraqqi
2.text:
Founded in 1966 by Mohammad Hashim Maiwandwal, prime minister from 1965 to 1967 and a former ambassador to Washington, the Progressive Democratic Party speaks through its newspaper Mosawat. Like every Afghan party it works without legal recognition, and since Maiwandwal's resignation it has been an opposition of notables, officials and urban professionals.

Its creed of progressive democracy blends evolutionary socialism, Islamic ethics and parliamentary government: land and tax reform, state-led development and a free press, but no class struggle. Maiwandwal is regarded as friendly to the West and keeps his distance from Moscow. The party's leverage lies in his prestige and in the educated middle class of Kabul and Kandahar.

3.name: Afghān Mellat
3.text:
Afghan Mellat ('Afghan Nation') was founded in 1966 by Ghulam Mohammad Farhad, the German-educated former mayor of Kabul who modernised the capital's streets and services. Formally a social democratic party, it is unlicensed like all others but well organised among Pashtun officials, teachers and students.

Its programme pairs social reform, state planning and mass education with fierce Pashtun nationalism: it demands the recovery of the Pashtun lands under Pakistan and the primacy of Pashto in state and school. It is anti-communist, hostile to Pakistan and distrustful of both superpowers. Its leverage lies in the Pashtun bureaucracy and the nationalist intelligentsia of Kabul and Kandahar.

4.name: Hezb-e Demokrātik-e Khalq-e Afghānistān (Parcham)
4.text:
The Parcham ('Banner') wing of the People's Democratic Party of Afghanistan takes its name from the weekly it published in 1968 and 1969. It emerged when the party founded in 1965 split in 1967, and is led by Babrak Karmal, re-elected to the Wolesi Jirga for Kabul in 1969, with Anahita Ratebzad, Mir Akbar Khyber and Sultan Ali Keshtmand. It is tolerated but unlicensed.

Parcham follows the Soviet line of national democracy: a broad front of workers, intellectuals and patriotic officers to lead Afghanistan onto a non-capitalist path with Soviet help. It recruits among urban, Persian-speaking intellectuals, civil servants and officers, and courts Daoud's circle. Moscow regards it as the more reliable partner.

5.name: Hezb-e Demokrātik-e Khalq-e Afghānistān (Khalq)
5.text:
The Khalq ('Masses') wing of the PDPA, named after the short-lived party newspaper of 1966, is led by the writer Nur Muhammad Taraki, the party's founding general secretary, and the ambitious teacher Hafizullah Amin, elected to the Wolesi Jirga in 1969. Since the 1967 split it has organised in schools, colleges and the officer corps.

Khalq rejects alliances with the feudal establishment and preaches class struggle and a swift revolution led by a vanguard of Pashtun teachers, students and junior officers from rural and lower-middle-class families. It is loyal to the Soviet Union but impatient with Moscow's caution. Its leverage is discipline, secrecy and its growing cells in the army.

6.name: Pashtunistān-khwāhān
6.text:
The Pashtunistan cause unites officials, tribal leaders, army officers and journalists who reject the Durand Line and demand self-determination for the Pashtuns and Baluch of Pakistan. It was state policy under Prime Minister Daoud and led to the border closure and near-war with Pakistan of 1961 to 1963. The court has cooled it since, but Pashtunistan Day is still celebrated every 31 August.

The irredentists see Pakistan's American alliance through SEATO and CENTO as the main threat and value Moscow, which has backed the Afghan claim since 1955, as the indispensable patron. They want a firmer nationalist government and more Soviet arms. Their leverage lies in the frontier tribes and the Pashtun officer corps.

7.name: Halqa-ye Sardār Dāwud
7.text:
Mohammed Daoud Khan, the king's cousin and brother-in-law, ran Afghanistan as prime minister from 1953 to 1963 and brought in Soviet arms and aid. The 1964 constitution's ban on royal relatives in government was aimed at him, and he now waits in his Kabul residence, receiving former ministers, nationalist officers and Parcham leaders who see him as the strongman the monarchy lacks.

The circle wants a centralised, modernising state led from above: planned development, a stronger army, the Pashtunistan claim pressed against Pakistan and close cooperation with Moscow. It despises parliament as a talking shop. Its leverage lies in Daoud's prestige among Soviet-trained officers and in the bureaucracy he built.

8.name: Mahfil-e Chindāwol
8.text:
In Chindawol, the Qizilbash and Hazara quarter of old Kabul, Shia notables, teachers and Najaf-trained clerics meet in husseiniyas and religious associations; the best-known reformist preacher is Mohammad Asef Mohseni of Kandahar. Shia Afghans have long faced discrimination, and their organisations remain cultural, since political Shiism has no legal outlet.

The circle seeks schools, publishing and equal citizenship for the Shia within the constitutional monarchy, and recognition of Jafari jurisprudence. It is loyal to the throne and wary of communists and Sunni Islamists alike. Its strength lies among educated Qizilbash civil servants and Hazara labourers in Kabul, and in its links to the seminaries of Najaf and Qom.

9.name: Talaba-ye Najaf
9.text:
A growing number of Afghan Shia study in the seminaries of Najaf and Qom, where Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini has lived in exile since 1965. The most radical of them, young Hazaras such as Abdul Ali Mazari, return to the Hazarajat convinced that the monarchy and the Pashtun khans who dominate it will never grant the Shia equality.

They preach that Islam is a complete political order, that the clergy must guide the community, and that the Hazara peasantry must be freed from landlords, nomad grazing rights and state neglect. Hostile to both superpowers and to Kabul's secular reforms, they are still few. Their leverage is the mosque network of the Hazarajat.

10.name: Hazrat-e Shor Bāzār
10.text:
The Mojaddedi family, the hereditary Hazrats of Shor Bazaar in Kabul, lead the Naqshbandi Sufi order and form the country's most influential religious dynasty. They helped bring Nadir Shah to the throne in 1929 and remain pillars of the royal religious establishment, although Sibghatullah Mojaddedi was imprisoned from 1959 to 1964 for plotting against Khrushchev's visit.

The family defends sharia courts, the authority of the ulema and the Hanafi character of the state, opposes communist and secular propaganda, and expects the king to protect Islam in return for its loyalty. Its leverage lies in thousands of Sufi disciples, rural mullahs and tribal leaders across the east and south.

11.name: Jihādiyān-e Pohantun
11.text:
The most militant Islamist students at Kabul University believe that lectures and pamphlets are not enough. Among them is the engineering student Gulbuddin Hekmatyar, who argues that the communists on campus must be fought physically and that the monarchy itself is un-Islamic.

Inspired by Sayyid Qutb and Abul A'la Maududi, they call for an Islamic revolution, a state governed by sharia and jihad against communism and Western corruption, and they look to like-minded Islamists in Pakistan and Egypt. They are few but disciplined, recruit among Pashtun students from the provinces, and their leverage lies in street fights, secret cells and the fear they inspire among leftist students.

12.name: Sāzmān-e Jawānān-e Musalmān
12.text:
Founded in 1969 by Islamist students at Kabul University to counter the PDPA and the Maoists, the Muslim Youth Organization is guided by the faculty of Islamic law, above all Professor Ghulam Mohammad Niazi and the young lecturer Burhanuddin Rabbani, back from al-Azhar. Its best-known student leader is Abdul Rahim Niazi.

Modelled on the Muslim Brotherhood, it translates Qutb and Maududi, contests student elections and demands an Islamic order in place of both secular reform and Marxism. It is anti-communist, suspicious of the West and critical of the court's moral laxity. Its leverage is the campus, provincial madrasa graduates and a disciplined, growing cadre.

13.name: Shurā-ye Wazirān
13.text:
Executive power under the 1964 constitution lies with a cabinet appointed by the king. Since 1967 it has been led by Nur Ahmad Etemadi, a career diplomat from a Kabul notable family, heading a government of technocrats and senior civil servants who manage the Third Five-Year Plan and the competing aid of both superpowers.

The government's creed is cautious, top-down development and strict non-alignment: Soviet roads, gas and military aid in the north, American dams, roads and schools in the south. It tolerates parliament but rarely takes it seriously. Its leverage lies in the ministries, the provincial governors and control of the foreign aid that funds most investment.

14.name: Khānān-e Jirga
14.text:
The Wolesi Jirga elected in 1969 is dominated by landowners, tribal khans and religious notables who won their seats through kinship and patronage rather than parties. They are the voice of rural Afghanistan in Kabul, blocking budgets and summoning ministers, but they have no programme beyond the interests of their districts.

They defend customary law, land ownership and the autonomy of tribes and villages against tax collectors, land registration and secular schooling, while expecting roads, water and offices from the state. They are loyal to the king and suspicious of the urban left. Their leverage lies in the votes they deliver and the armed tribesmen they can mobilise.

15.name: Bānk-e Milli-ye Afghān
15.text:
Bank-e Milli, founded in the early 1930s by the entrepreneur Abdul Majid Zabuli, stands at the centre of a web of joint-stock companies that dominate the export trade in karakul skins, cotton and dried fruit and own textile mills and other early industries. Its shareholders include leading merchant families of Kabul, Kandahar and Herat, and senior officials.

The bank's circle favours a mixed economy in which state concessions and monopolies protect private profit. It welcomes Western credit and trade but deals pragmatically with Soviet barter, and it opposes land reform and nationalisation. Its leverage lies in money: it finances the state, its projects and many of its officials.

16.name: Sarāy-e Shahzāda
16.text:
Sarai Shahzada, the walled money bazaar beside the Kabul River, is the heart of Afghanistan's private finance. Its hawala dealers, moneychangers and transit traders, many of them Hindu, Sikh and Pashtun merchants, move funds and goods between Kabul, Peshawar, the Gulf and Central Asia beyond the reach of the state.

They want low duties, a freely convertible afghani, unrestricted transit trade and an end to state monopolies and export controls. They distrust both planned development and Soviet barter. Their leverage is that much of the country's trade and credit, and much of the smuggling across the Pakistani border, flows through their ledgers.

17.name: Dostān-e Band-e Amir
17.text:
Foresters, agronomists and Kabul University scientists, working alongside United Nations advisers, have begun to warn of what development is doing to the land. They campaign for the protection of the turquoise lakes of Band-e Amir in the Hindu Kush and against the felling of the eastern forests and the salinisation of the American-built irrigation schemes in the Helmand valley.

They want national parks, forest laws, controlled grazing and careful water management in place of prestige dams. Hostile to neither bloc, they rely on international agencies. They have no popular base, but their reports reach ministers, and Band-e Amir is a source of national and royal pride.

18.name: Setam-e Melli
18.text:
Setam-e Melli ('National Oppression') is the movement of Tahir Badakhshi, a Tajik founding member of the PDPA central committee who broke with Taraki in 1967 and 1968 over what he saw as Pashtun chauvinism in the party. It organises clandestinely among Tajik, Uzbek and Hazara students, teachers and officials, especially in Badakhshan and the north.

It argues that Afghanistan's real contradiction is the domination of the non-Pashtun nationalities by a Pashtun state and court, and calls for socialism, land reform and the federal equality of all peoples. It is independent of Moscow and drawn to Chinese ideas of rural struggle. Its leverage lies in the northern provinces and among non-Pashtun intellectuals.

19.name: Sāzmān-e Jawānān-e Motaraqqi
19.text:
The Progressive Youth Organization, founded in 1965 by Akram Yari and the Mahmudi brothers, is better known by its newspaper Shola-e Javid ('Eternal Flame'), banned in 1968. Its followers, the Sholais, led the student demonstrations that shook Kabul University and the high schools in 1968 and 1969, and they agitate among Kabul's workers.

They are Maoists: they denounce the PDPA as revisionist lackeys of Soviet social-imperialism, reject parliament and preach a people's war of peasants against landlords and the monarchy. Recruiting strongly among Hazara, Tajik and Shia students, they look to Beijing. Their leverage is the campus, the street and the provincial schools.

20.name: Mullāhā-ye Deh
20.text:
Outside Kabul, village and small-town mullahs voice a countryside angered by unveiled women in the capital, co-educational schools, leftist student marches and rising prices. They stood behind the Kandahar riots of 1959 against the unveiling policy and now preach Friday sermons against the godless newspapers tolerated under the 1965 press law.

Their populism is religious and anti-urban: they demand that the government close leftist papers, punish blasphemy, keep women at home and spare the poor from new taxes. They distrust the Russians, the Americans and Kabul's officials alike. Their leverage is the pulpit and the ability to bring angry crowds into the streets.

21.name: Āryānā-parastān
21.text:
Since the 1930s the Afghan state has taught that Afghanistan is ancient Aryana, cradle of the Aryans, an idea absorbed by officers and officials trained in Germany before the war and by today's nationalist students. A small ultranationalist fringe takes it to extremes, glorifying race, martial virtue and a Greater Afghanistan from the Oxus to the Indus.

It calls for a one-party national state, Pashtun cultural supremacy, the reconquest of Pashtunistan and the purging of foreign-inspired communists and Islamists alike. It admires strong men and German discipline and despises both blocs. It has no organisation of its own and works through nationalist circles, schools and the officer corps.

22.name: Qowwā-ye Mosallah-e Shāhi-ye Afghānistān
22.text:
The Royal Afghan Army and Air Force number around 80,000 men, equipped almost entirely with Soviet tanks, artillery and MiG fighters since the arms deals of 1956. Thousands of officers have trained in the Soviet Union, a smaller group in the United States, Turkey and India. Under the 1964 constitution the forces are apolitical and loyal to the king.

The senior command is royalist and Pashtun, but junior officers resent low pay, slow promotion and the royal family's monopoly of top posts, and both Daoud and the PDPA are courting them. The army's leverage is simple: it is the only force that can make or break the throne.

23.name: Khāndān-e Bārakzay
23.text:
Mohammed Zahir Shah has reigned since his father Nadir Shah's assassination in 1933, first under his uncles and then his cousin Daoud as prime ministers. Since 1963 he has ruled in person, and the 1964 constitution launched his New Democracy: an elected parliament, a freer press and a ban on royal relatives holding office. The Musahiban branch of the Barakzai still controls the court, army and key provinces.

The king governs by balancing Soviet and American aid, tribes and technocrats, clerics and students. He has never signed the law on political parties and keeps final authority over government. The crown's leverage is legitimacy, the army's loyalty and patronage.
